transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi doctor. Well, I'm here because... honestly, it's just getting to be too much to handle. I work as a host at a restaurant and lounge, and I'm the first person people see when they walk in the door, right? So presentation is a big part of the job. But I just... I cannot stop thinking about my hairline and the way my face looks, especially under those specific restaurant lights. 

They have these overhead pendant lights right above the host stand, and I am just constantly agonizing over how they make me look so old and... strange. Like, my hairline looks so glaring and receding, and the shadows make my facial features just look bizarre and distorted. It's all I can focus on. I'll be standing there, supposed to be smiling and taking reservations, but my mind is just racing, completely fixated on how awful and weird my face looks to everyone walking in. 

I've actually asked my coworkers about it a lot. I'll ask them, you know, "Hey, does this light make my forehead look weird?" or "Do I look terrible standing in this spot?" and they always tell me they absolutely don't see what I'm talking about. They just brush it off and say I look totally fine, just like a normal guy. But I feel like they're just being polite, because I know what's there. And it's just exhausting, doctor, because I can't turn these thoughts off for even a single minute while I'm trying to work. It just plays on a loop in my head all night.
Do these concerns about your appearance bother you even when you're not at work or under different lighting conditions, like when you're at home or out with friends?

Oh, God, yes. It’s not just the restaurant. I mean, the restaurant is where I feel the most exposed because I'm literally paid to be the face at the door, but... it’s everywhere. It follows me home, it’s there the second I wake up. Just getting out of the house is an absolute nightmare now. I’ll spend hours—and I mean literally hours—just standing in my bathroom, trying to adjust my hair, trying to see if there's some angle, any angle at all, where my face doesn't look so... so distorted and old. 

And because of that, because I just get trapped in this cycle of looking and trying to fix it and feeling awful, I’ve actually been written up at work. Multiple times, actually. I end up being late for my shifts because I just can't pull myself away from the mirror, or sometimes I just call out and miss my shifts entirely because I absolutely cannot stomach the idea of anyone looking at me that day. It's humiliating to be a 54-year-old man getting reprimanded like a teenager for attendance, but I just can't stop it. 

And as for my personal life... it's basically nonexistent at this point. You asked about friends, and... well, I’ve completely stopped going to things. At work, we used to do these group staff photos, and I refuse to be anywhere near them now. I can't even look at a camera without panicking. And outside of work, I used to love going to gallery events in the city, or going on hikes with people on the weekends, getting some fresh air. But I just can't do it anymore. I’ve stopped going to all of it because I just can’t handle being seen that way. The thought of people looking at my receding hairline or the weird shadows on my face while we're just supposed to be enjoying a hike in the daylight... it makes my chest tight just thinking about it. So I just stay home. I isolate myself because it feels like the only way I don't have to obsess over how hideous I look to the rest of the world.
Do you believe that the way your hairline and facial features look under the lights means that you are physically unattractive or deformed in some way?

Unattractive is... well, unattractive is such a mild word for it, doctor. I mean, when I look in the mirror, or when I catch a reflection of myself on one of the glass doors at work... I don't just see a guy who maybe isn't conventionally handsome, you know? I see someone who is fundamentally broken to look at. Deformed is exactly the word I would use. It's like... it's like my hairline isn't just a normal receding hairline that guys my age get, it's this glaring, almost alien feature that completely throws off the entire proportion of my head. It makes my forehead look completely misshapen. And then my face, the way the shadows hit... it makes me look like some kind of ghoul. 

I'll just stand there in the bathroom for hours, analyzing the way the skin seems to hang or the way the bone structure just looks completely wrong, completely unnatural. And I know people say they don't see it, like my coworkers I mentioned, but I know they have to be lying or just trying to spare my feelings because it is so incredibly obvious. How could they not see it? It's right there. It's literally all I can see. I mean, if you saw exactly what I see when I look in the mirror, you'd understand why I can't even leave the house sometimes, why I miss my shifts. It's not just vanity or wanting to look nice for a shift. It's this deep, horrifying realization that I am physically repulsive to look at. 

Every single person who walks into that lounge is forced to look at this... this deformed face before they even get to their table, and honestly, it makes me feel so guilty. I feel like I'm subjecting them to something awful just by standing there doing my job. Because it really is a deformity to me. It's grotesque. I just... I don't understand how anyone could look at me and not be completely put off by how strange and ugly my features are. It just consumes everything I think about.
Have you noticed any other changes or issues with your body that concern you, or is it mainly your hairline and facial features that cause you distress?

Other issues? No, no, not really. I mean... my body is just... it's a normal body. I don't really pay attention to my stomach or my arms or my legs or anything like that. It's... it's entirely my face and my hairline. 

Because, you see, doctor, you can cover up a body, right? If you don't like your stomach, you just buy a looser shirt or wear a sweater. At the restaurant, I wear this very nice, dark, tailored blazer, and it looks sharp. It looks professional. But my face... my face is just completely exposed to the world. There's absolutely no hiding it. I can't put a bag over my head when I'm greeting guests, as much as I might want to. I'll be standing there at the front, holding these heavy, leather-bound dinner menus—we use these really nice textured ones for the evening service—and I'll look down at my hands, and I'll think, "Okay, my hands look fine. They just look like normal, 54-year-old hands." 

But then I'll catch my reflection in the polished brass lamp sitting on the podium, or I'll see myself in the glass of the front double doors when it's dark outside, and it all just comes rushing back. Bam. The forehead. The shadows. The way my features are just so twisted and wrong. It’s like my brain just zeroes in on that one specific area, from the top of my glaring, alien scalp right down to my chin, and it just gets stuck there on a loop. I honestly think I could have a third arm growing out of my shoulder and I wouldn't even notice it, because I am so entirely, completely consumed by how grotesque my head looks. 

So, no, I don't worry about the rest of my body at all. It's just the face. It's always the face. It just takes up all the space in my head, every single second of the day, and there's just no room left to care about anything else.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a long-standing, persistent preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance—specifically, his hairline and facial features—accompanied by repetitive behaviors (mirror checking), significant distress, and functional impairment across occupational and social domains. He exhibits a firm conviction that others perceive him as grotesquely deformed, despite reassurance from others and no objective evidence of such a defect.
